article_content: NBC News anchor Brian Williams issued a swift on-air apology Wednesday after Arsenio Hall criticized his exclusion from a list of influential late-night TV personalities. 'Arsenio is a late-night veteran, and he rightfully called us out on his show, even encouraging his audience to contact our newsroom,' Williams stated during his 'Nightly News' broadcast from the Winter Olympics in Sochi. Hall's prompting was direct. He not only urged his viewers to phone NBC News but also featured rap mogul Suge Knight, quipping, 'Sometimes I take a joke too far.' Oops: Brian Williams apologized from Sochi on Wednesday for omitting Arsenio Hall, a talk show veteran, from a list of prominent late-night figures—who were all white and, in many cases, less experienced than Hall. 'Let me be in the middle where Alice used to be': Hall's displeasure stemmed from a 'Brady Bunch'-like montage showcasing late-night hosts. Hours later, Williams addressed the issue, humorously referencing other network errors. 'In apologizing to Arsenio, we want to highlight that he's in good company,' Williams remarked. He noted that the newscast had previously omitted New Hampshire from a map and, on Tuesday, misspelled Philadelphia on-screen. Hall's exclusion occurred during what he termed NBC News' ‘Brady Bunch montage,’ which displayed photos of numerous late-night TV hosts, including David Letterman, Chelsea Handler, and Carson Daly. Hall's initial reaction involved jokes about the segment's all-white composition, and he encouraged viewers to call the NBC newsroom. 'We might be kidding, Brian. Sometimes I take a joke too far. Just mention me, man,' Hall joked after Suge Knight made veiled threats onstage. The graphic was featured in Monday's ‘Nightly News’ segment about Jimmy Fallon's ‘The Tonight Show’ debut, also on NBC. On Tuesday's ‘The Arsenio Hall Show,’ Hall, though smiling, expressed his irritation while displaying the graphic and criticizing Williams and journalism in general. 'If you're reporting on late-night television, I only ask that you mention me,' Hall stated. 'You don't even need to use a photo. I understand journalism these days. Use Samuel Jackson—it doesn't even have to be my photo. Use Laurence Fishburne. Just mention me.' Hall referenced the actors involved in a recent media error where a TV reporter mistook Jackson for Fishburne. Both are black. Arsenio Hall successfully hosted a talk show that competed with Johnny Carson and attracted notable guests, including then-President Bill Clinton. The late-night landscape is predominantly white, with few exceptions such as Hall and PBS' Tavis Smiley. 'There's not even anyone with a tan,' Hall commented on the NBC News montage. Hall, noting that he is the only current late-night host 'who competed and survived against Johnny Carson,' stated he held no animosity toward other hosts. Hall's new show premiered in September; his original late-night show ran from 1989 to 1994, concurrent with Carson's tenure on ‘Tonight.’ Declining to play the 'angry black man,' Hall invited Suge Knight onstage to encourage Williams and others in journalism to 'include a brother.' Knight suggested giving Williams time to respond before pursuing further action. 'Change it or resign?' Hall responded. 'We might just be kidding, Brian. Sometimes I take a joke too far. Just mention me, man.' Following Williams' apology, Hall graciously accepted it. 'That was a cool way to do,' Hall said on his show Wednesday. 'Thanks, Brian! I appreciate it.'

article_content: Across the U.S., cities are working hard to manage a surge in public transport use as gas prices stay high. Data shows that recent elevated gas prices have significantly influenced how people commute. Even areas known for car reliance and limited public transit are seeing more people use mass transit. The American Public Transportation Association reports growth across all types of public transit, from trains to buses. Cities are adopting different strategies to handle this increased ridership, according to an APTA survey. For instance, the Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority is increasing its fleet of subway cars and buses. The Charlotte Area Transit System in North Carolina has increased weekend light rail service. The Southeastern Pennsylvania Transportation Authority is adding new hybrid buses (400) and rail cars (120) to accommodate increased ridership. Transit systems are also adjusting schedules and creating bus-only lanes. Denver's transit system faces a financial challenge due to reduced sales tax revenue because of high fuel costs. Cal Marsella describes this as the 'paradox of public transportation,' where demand is highest when funding is limited. The Denver Regional Transit District managed to secure diesel fuel at $3.20 a gallon earlier this year. Americans used public transit a lot more in the first three months of the year. They took 2.6 billion trips, which is 85 million more than last year. People also drove less, with 1.4 billion fewer highway miles recorded. Cynthia Stabb from Tulsa Transit notes that ridership stays high even after gas prices decrease. Dr. Robert Lang suggests that the gas price situation could change how people see public transit. He mentions Denver and Phoenix as examples where residents supported transportation projects despite the cost. Atlanta is finding it harder to adapt due to disagreements about transit expansion. Mayor Shirley Franklin notes the need for an integrated transport system. Lang acknowledges the importance of cars in American culture but suggests a future with both hybrid cars and better transit. He speculates that 2007 might be the year with the most gas use in the U.S.

article_content: Travelers will now be allowed to bring golf clubs, ski poles, and even small knives on planes, as aviation officials have announced significant security changes. A number of previously banned items will be permitted for the first time since the September 11th terrorist attacks, sparking concern from flight attendants who stated the decision could endanger passengers and crew. The TSA stated that, effective April 25, it would allow small knives with blades 2.36 inches or less in length and less than 1/2 inch wide. Flight attendants are expressing concerns about the new changes that will lift a number of prohibitions and allow travelers to carry small knives on board. TSA officials hope that maintaining certain restrictions will alleviate fear among travelers. Other items that will be allowed on board again as part of a passenger's carry-on luggage include billiard cues, ski poles, hockey sticks, and lacrosse sticks. Items that had been prohibited, like razors, box cutters, or knives with a fixed blade, are still not allowed on board. The restrictions regarding liquids remain in place, meaning anything under 3 ounces must be declared at the security checkpoint. TSA spokesman David Castelveter said the decision was made to better align U.S. regulations with International Civil Aviation Organization standards and to provide a better experience for travelers. The TSA says the changes reflect the findings of their recent review of security measures. The Association of Professional Flight Attendants 'categorically rejects' a proposal to allow knives of any kind in the cabin and questions why 'such a momentous decision' was made without any consultation. They added that allowing larger items, such as sports equipment, increases 'the potential for passengers getting hit with these items during boarding and deplaning,' calling it 'a recipe for disaster.' Castelveter said, 'This is part of an overall Risk-Based Security approach, which allows Transportation Security officers to better focus their efforts on finding higher-threat items such as explosives.' The Flight Attendants Union Coalition, representing nearly 90,000 flight attendants from carriers across the country, called the decision a 'poor and shortsighted decision' by the TSA. TSA officials have changed their stance on certain prohibited objects, which will now be allowed on planes starting on April 25. Billiard cues and lacrosse sticks will now be permitted on board. The coalition stated, 'As the last line of defense in the cabin and key aviation partners, we believe that these proposed changes will further endanger the lives of all flight attendants and the passengers we work so hard to keep safe and secure.' Castelveter said the TSA has implemented a number of safety measures, including reinforced cockpit doors, allowing some pilots to be armed, and federal air marshals on board airplanes. He said those measures would help ensure the safety of passengers and crew. After the September 11, 2001, hijacking attacks, the U.S. government imposed strict guidelines for what could be carried on board an aircraft - some of which differed from what other countries allowed passengers to carry on airplanes.

article_content: If it seems like nearly everyone you see these days, from kids to seniors, has some kind of tech gadget handy, it's not just your imagination. According to a new report from the Pew Internet and American Life Project, approximately 90% of Americans now own a cell phone, computer, MP3 player, game console, e-reader, or tablet. In 'Generations and Their Gadgets,' Pew explores how different age groups in the U.S. use their tech devices. It defines six generations ranging from age 18 to 75-plus. Eighty-five percent of Americans own cell phones, making them the most popular type of tech gadget. Slightly more Americans use their cell phones to take pictures (76%) than to send or receive text messages (72%); however, across all age groups, these two activities are the most popular non-voice call functions. Among the 15% of Americans who do not own a cell phone, one-third live in a household with at least one working cell phone. Overall, '90% of all adults (including 62% of those age 75 and older) live in a household with at least one working cell phone,' according to the survey. Pew notes that as of June, about a quarter of all U.S. households had gone mobile-only, forgoing traditional landline phone connections. This includes more than half of all adults ages 25 to 29, highlighting the need to update the U.S. 911 emergency calling system to be more cell phone-friendly and accommodate more types of communication than voice calls. Even though more people are getting smartphones (estimated 30 percent of U.S. cell phone owners), Americans ages 18 to 34 are especially likely to use their phones for various purposes: internet access, e-mail, games, music, sending/receiving photos, recording video, etc. The only widely popular activities across all age groups are taking pictures and text messaging, which may explain why 70% of Americans still rely on non-smart 'feature phones,' which have fewer features. As tech gadgets go, MP3 players are relatively limited devices. It's somewhat surprising that the youngest and most tech-savvy age group Pew studied is the most likely to own an MP3 player. Three-quarters of Americans ages 18 to 34 own an MP3 player, but only 56% of the next oldest group (35 to 46) do. As of September, 5% of U.S. adults owned tablets such as the iPad or Galaxy Tab, up from 3% in May. (Apple's iPad was launched in U.S. stores in April.) With the launch of several Android-based iPad competitors, this type of device is expected to become more popular. It will be interesting to see if tablet ownership starts to displace laptop ownership. Currently, 5% of Americans own e-readers such as the Kindle or Nook, but this underestimates the total number of people who read e-books. Many people read e-books on their smartphones, tablets, and desktop or laptop computers. E-readers are most popular among Americans ages 47 to 56. It is suspected that in the next year, tablets will impact patterns of mobile device ownership and use in the U.S. If tablet prices decrease and more options for size and connectivity emerge (especially for Android models), many people who primarily rely on feature phones might choose to invest in a Wi-Fi-enabled tablet (a one-time expense) rather than upgrading to a full smartphone (with higher monthly bills and potential unexpected charges). The opinions expressed in this story are solely those of Amy Gahran.

article_content: Michaella McCollum Connolly, 20, and Melissa Reid, 19, both British, are detained in Peru, accused of attempting to smuggle £1.5 million of cocaine. Reports suggest they've refused food for a week, exhibiting terror and hysteria since their arrest. Suspected of cartel links, they are in high-security cells. They claimed summer jobs in Ibiza, but 11kg of cocaine were found in their luggage at Lima airport. A conviction could mean up to 25 years in a severe Peruvian prison. Shocked families are traveling to Peru for support. Santa Monica prison near Lima, overcrowded and dangerous, is a potential destination if convicted.

article_content: In Khartoum, Sudan, public anger erupted following a YouTube video depicting Sudanese police officers laughing while publicly flogging a woman who was pleading and attempting to escape. This incident triggered demonstrations, leading to the arrest of 52 individuals, including 46 women and six men, for unlawful assembly according to the Khartoum State Police Force. They were later released on bail. The two-minute video has ignited widespread condemnation across Sudan, with pro-government newspaper columnists urging for a swift investigation, particularly focusing on the manner in which the flogging was conducted. The video shows a woman, wearing a head scarf and a black abaya, being instructed in Arabic to sit down in a parking lot to receive her punishment, allowing the officers to return home. Initially, the flogging was administered to her back, adhering to the Sharia code. However, when she turned and pleaded for mercy, the whipping continued on the front of her body, affecting her face, hands, and legs. A bystander, clearly shocked, exclaimed, 'There is no authority but God's' after witnessing the punishment. One officer responded by saying, 'This is a fundamental principle. Let him whip her.' The video further reveals an officer laughing upon realizing he was being filmed, inviting the person behind the camera to record spectators he claimed were laughing along. This officer then participated in the flogging, with the woman being whipped by both officers. Adel Al-Agib, Sudan's deputy police chief, initially tried to minimize the situation, stating to the government's news agency that the video was disseminated to tarnish the country's image. During a meeting organized by the Sudanese Journalism and Publications Council, Al-Agib claimed the video was recorded in July 2009 but released recently to coincide with International Human Rights Day, aiming to increase international pressure on Sudan. On Sunday, the Judiciary Authority, responsible for overseeing the legal system, announced the launch of an inquiry to determine if the punishment was administered incorrectly, without addressing the punishment's justification itself. The judiciary authority stated it would investigate whether the 'execution of a punishment went against legally established guidelines according to criminal publications.' According to their statement, 'The investigation was started immediately after the images of the young woman, being punished under Articles 154 and 155 of the 1991 Sudanese penal code, appeared on the internet.' Article 154 pertains to 'the practice of prostitution,' and Article 155 addresses 'the management of a place of prostitution.' Authorities have not released specific details regarding the woman's alleged offenses. Local news sources indicate that the flogging occurred in Omdurman, Khartoum's sister city across the river, at the Kajabab Police Station, located in a poor neighborhood known for brothels and the illicit sale of 'aragi,' a local moonshine. Flogging is commonplace in northern Sudan, where Islamic law is often enforced arbitrarily under the Public Order Act. Police and 'public order units' possess the authority to enforce standards of dress and behavior. Local human rights organizations have consistently accused the police of abusing their power to mistreat women. A previous case involving Lubna Hussein, a former journalist who worked for the United Nations, gained international attention when she was arrested with other women for wearing trousers. Although found guilty, she was fined rather than flogged. The Public Order Act also applies to men. Last week, a court in Khartoum found seven men guilty of indecency for wearing make-up at the 'Sudanese Next Top Model fashion show.' They were each fined 200 Sudanese pounds, equivalent to $60. CNN's Michael Martinez contributed to this report.

article_content: MSNBC news anchor Melissa Harris-Perry has ignited controversy with a TV advertisement promoting the network. In the ad, she suggests that children belong to communities, not solely to their parents. Harris-Perry, who hosts a Sunday morning MSNBC show bearing her name, created the promotional spot to promote her program. The statement has drawn criticism from conservative commentators Sarah Palin and Glenn Beck. 'We have never invested as much in public education as we should have,' Harris-Perry says in the ad, 'because we've always had a somewhat private notion of children: 'Your kid is yours, and entirely your responsibility.' We haven't embraced a collective notion of 'these are our children.' 'So, in part, we must overcome our private notion that kids belong exclusively to their parents or families and recognize that kids belong to whole communities.' Sarah Palin and Glenn Beck criticized MSNBC host Melissa Harris-Perry for suggesting that communities, rather than individual parents, bear the primary responsibility for raising children. article_content: Giant pandas attract considerable attention in efforts to protect species from extinction, largely due to their appealing appearance, despite their low reproductive rates. The Ugly Animal Preservation Society aims to increase awareness of less conventionally attractive species. 'We care so much about mammals – especially cute, furry, and cuddly things,' Simon Watt, president of the society, stated at The Times Cheltenham Science Festival. The proboscis monkey, an endangered species, is often overlooked by conservationists because it lacks the 'cuteness' factor of pandas. Similarly, the Myers' Surinam toad, threatened by habitat loss, receives little support due to its 'on the point of death' appearance. Watt argues that focusing solely on charismatic megafauna leads to a less diverse and interesting world. The giant panda has been the logo of the World Wide Fund for Nature since 1961. Zoos worldwide implement breeding programs to encourage panda reproduction, often with limited success. Watt highlighted the Myers' Surinam toad, noting its resemblance to a road accident victim. Although healthy, its appearance suggests imminent death, and its population faces similar threats to tigers but receives far less attention. Pandas dominate global conservation efforts due to their perceived cuddliness, despite their limited activity. The pthirus pubis, or crab louse, faces extinction due to the prevalence of pubic hair waxing. The proboscis monkey, with its distinctive long nose, suffers from neglect despite its critically endangered status. Its habitat in Borneo is diminishing, resulting in a 50% population decrease in the last 40 years. Scientist Jamie Gallagher championed the Chinese giant salamander, the world's largest amphibian, at the festival. He noted its neglect as the animal is consumed into extinction, with South China having decimated 75% of its population. The Ugly Animal Preservation Society asserts that protecting only cute animals would impoverish the world, referencing the Spanish Dancer sea slug. The Chinese giant salamander is being eaten into extinction. In January, the plight of pubic lice was highlighted when a Sydney sexual health clinic reported no cases of crabs since 2008, attributing it to bikini waxing. 'It used to be extremely common; it’s now rarely seen,' said Basil Donovan, head of sexual health at the University of New South Wales’s Kirby Institute and a physician at the Sydney Sexual Health Centre. 'Without doubt, it’s better grooming.' The Ugly Animals Preservation Society hosts stand-up comedy events to advocate for ugly and neglected species.

article_content: PLAYA DEL REY, California (CNN) -- A black sedan pulled into the parking lot at Dockweiler State Beach in California, and the five members of The Lost Trailers emerged -- no chauffeur, publicist, manager, or entourage. The band members, from left to right, are Jeff Potter, Stokes Nielson, Ryder Lee, Manny Medina, and Andrew Nielson. This is how the rising country band operates these days. Their current 'Lean, Clean and Local' tour aims to streamline operations in an environmentally friendly way. Since September, they've reduced their carbon footprint by 132 tons by giving up tour buses and traveling with minimal road crew, bringing only essential equipment. Their new focus is 'hiring local' -- local roadies, T-shirt vendors, and suppliers for amps and equipment. If it can't fit in a suitcase, it stays behind. The Lost Trailers have also partnered with Keep America Beautiful, a national organization focused on litter reduction and recycling. During a recent day off in Los Angeles, singer Ryder Lee, guitarist Stokes Nielson, bassist Manny Medina, keyboardist Andrew Nielson, and drummer Jeff Potter joined a group of young adults from the L.A. Conservation Corps for a coastal cleanup. Three band members wore cowboy boots as they collected trash along the beach. The volunteers were from South Central Los Angeles, an area not particularly known for country music. After the cleanup, a CNN van played The Lost Trailers' hit single, 'Holler Back.' Initially, the students showed blank expressions during the fiddle and banjo intro. However, after joining in the chorus of 'heys' and 'hos,' a young man named Virgil LaFlora began rapping over the verses. This created an unexpected country/hip-hop fusion, reminiscent of Tim McGraw and Nelly's collaboration on 'Over and Over' in 2004. This shared musical experience created camaraderie, with the song ending in cheers and hugs. One girl requested a copy of the CD. CNN interviewed The Lost Trailers' members about their activism and tour. The following is an edited version of the interview. CNN: 'Lean, Clean and Local' involves more than just recycling. You're also actively hiring local people. Stokes Nielson: We performed with Tim McGraw in New York late last year. Since it was a fly date, we hired local crew. One individual thanked us for providing local employment, as he hadn't received a paycheck in three weeks. As the recession deepened, we realized we could support communities by hiring local talent, rather than extracting money with our own crew and leaving. This allows us to contribute a small stimulus to the local economy. CNN: As rising artists, you've worked hard to earn the right to a tour bus. Now you're giving it up. Stokes Nielson: By eliminating the bus and flying to dates, we minimized our diesel consumption. Andrew Nielson: We pack light to enable hiring local crews and equipment. Jeff Potter: Renting drums avoids the practical difficulties of transporting a drum set on a plane. It's convenient as a local crew sets everything up. Ryder Lee: We considered electric drum pads for portability, but they're not as appealing. CNN: A drum machine would be even more economical! Potter: I prefer playing with the band. Manny Medina: I worry about local bass players replacing me! (Laugh) CNN: Is hiring local more or less expensive? Stokes Nielson: It's about the same. This isn't primarily about money. The government is investing heavily in stimulating the economy. As small business owners, we want to contribute. It's rewarding to do something beyond writing and performing songs. Lee: We created LeanCleanAndLocal.com as a resource for local businesses. It features videos and a directory, allowing other acts to connect with these professionals. CNN: Does this ever lead to complications? Medina: So far, so good. Potter: We've been fortunate in working with competent professionals. As a national act, we appreciate the high level of expertise. CNN: You likely considered various organizations before partnering with Keep America Beautiful. Why them? Lee: Preserving our rural heritage is important to country artists. Protecting rivers and streams is part of our identity, and we're proud of it. Keep America Beautiful's focus on recycling and litter cleanup aligned with our values. Plus, our shows tend to generate a lot of bottles and cans! (Laugh) Stokes Nielson: This tour might be temporary, perhaps lasting until the recession ends. Regardless, we want to contribute positively. Medina: Hiring local deepens our connection with the towns we visit. We meet people, instead of staying isolated on the bus. We get to know the towns.

article_content: TEHRAN, Iran (CNN) -- Iranian pro-government Basij militia members dispersed crowds of protesters Thursday, sometimes using force, according to witnesses. These protests, similar to the one on June 15, have been supported by reformist figures. An estimated 2,000 to 3,000 people gathered in various locations and moved toward Tehran University, the site of a student uprising in 1999. Witnesses reported that several protesters were struck on their arms and backs by the Basij militia, while riot police deployed tear gas into the crowds. Iran's state-funded Press TV reported the crowd size near the university to be in the hundreds. Some protesters chanted 'Allahu Akbar,' meaning 'God is Great,' and 'Ya Hussein, Mir Hussein,' referring to opposition candidate Mir Hossein Moussavi. Police blocked roads leading to Tehran University, and some protesters set fire to trash cans to counteract the effects of the tear gas. Witnesses told CNN that when crowds attempted to assemble between 4 p.m. and 5 p.m. in Revolution Square, hundreds of security forces were present. Most security forces were uniformed officers wearing helmets and holding batons and shields, while others were in plain clothes. The forces instructed bystanders to move along, witnesses stated. At least five clashes were reported during this period. Over the next two hours, the crowds grew to approximately 3,000, but security forces also increased in number, according to witnesses. Many protesters left Revolution Square and marched to side streets and neighborhoods a few kilometers away, holding up victory signs and clapping. Several dumpsters were set on fire. Witnesses reported hearing sounds resembling gunshots and seeing security forces using what appeared to be pepper spray on the crowds. Chants heard included familiar refrains: 'Death to the Dictator!' 'Death to Khamenei!' A new phrase emerged: 'Mojtaba bemire, rahbariroh nagiri,' meaning 'Die, Mojtaba, so you don't become the supreme leader!' Rumors have circulated that Mojtaba has taken over the pro-government Basij militia and that his father is grooming him to be the next supreme leader. Thursday marked the first instance of protesters chanting against him. By nightfall, most demonstrators went home. At 10 p.m. Tehran time, two sources informed CNN that chants of 'God is great!' were louder than usual in their neighborhoods. The demonstration occurred on the 10th anniversary of a student uprising that posed a significant threat to the Islamic regime. Protesters used the anniversary to resume demonstrations against the outcome of the contested June 12 presidential election. Iranian-American journalist Jason Rezaian noted that Iranians have been fearful since last month's crackdown on protesters of the election results. Incumbent Mahmoud Ahmadinejad was declared the winner over reformist candidate Moussavi, who alleged the election was rigged. Moussavi's supporters protested in large numbers until the protests turned violent due to the security forces' crackdown. Iranian state-run media reported 20 deaths and over 1,000 detentions. On July 9, 1999, known as the 18th of Tir, 200 students protested the closing of a reformist newspaper, Salaam, which supported moderate President Mohammed Khatami. Hard-line activists entered dormitories in Tehran University, vandalized property, and attacked students, leading to six days of protests. Human Rights Watch stated that over 25,000 people participated, making the demonstrations the biggest threat to the Islamic regime since its inception in 1979. CNN's Reza Sayah and Moni Basu contributed to this report from Atlanta, Georgia.

article_content: In Mombasa, Kenya, anti-terror police have accused British authorities of disregarding warnings that Michael Adebolajo, a suspect in the Woolwich murder, was a dangerous radical. Adebolajo was apprehended in Kenya in 2010 on suspicion of plotting to cross into Somalia and join the Al Shabaab terrorist group. However, Kenyan officials claim that when they presented their evidence to the British Embassy, it was asserted that Adebolajo had no criminal record. Sources in Kenya also allege that the British Embassy pressured them to release Adebolajo after he complained of torture, starvation, and denial of access to legal counsel. Furthermore, another Kenyan source claimed that the British failed to assist them in building a case against Adebolajo. Adebolajo was detained for several days before being deported back to the UK. These allegations surfaced as Adebolajo’s family claimed that harassment by MI5 in the months preceding the attack might have ‘pushed him over the edge’. Family members assert that upon his return to the UK from Kenya, he was ‘pestered’ by MI5 agents who attempted to recruit him as an informant to infiltrate Islamic extremist groups. Adebolajo’s brother-in-law, Abu Zuybyr, stated that the intelligence services pressured Adebolajo to spy on Muslim clerics and become an informer. Mr. Zuybyr, married to Adebolajo’s sister Christiana, said: ‘That is what [Adebolajo’s] family is saying: that the secret service pushed him over the edge.’ He added that Adebolajo was ‘elated’ after the birth of his child, but ‘then things became a little strange’. Speaking to The Independent on Sunday, Mr. Zuybyr said Adebolajo traveled to Nairobi in 2010 to study Arabic and Islam. Following his return to England, Mr. Zuybyr said authorities repeatedly questioned family members about Adebolajo. His elder brother, Jeremiah, who had gone to Saudi Arabia to teach English, was arrested and questioned. Mr. Zuybyr also mentioned being questioned at gunpoint when he visited Yemen four years prior to learn Arabic with his wife. He stated: ‘When I came back to Britain, MI5 contacted me and showed significant interest in Michael. I was harassed for a while, with constant calls from people claiming to be from the FBI.’ In Kenya, Adebolajo was seized with five others, along with a married couple who owned a guest house where they had been staying, and a worker, after traveling by speedboat to an island off the coast near Lamu Island, approximately 68 miles from the Somali border. Kenyan authorities believed Adebolajo, then 28, had played a crucial role in recruiting his co-accused, including two secondary school-aged boys, after they were radicalized during weekly visits to a mosque in Mombasa. It is believed that the Kenyan cleric Sheikh Aboud Rogo – who was killed by gunmen in Mombasa the previous year – had helped to fund the men. Adebolajo was eventually deported without charge, but Kenyan officials insist they warned the British that he was dangerous. Mombasa’s anti-terrorist police chief, Elijah Rop, stated: ‘We advised the British police about the man but they ignored us.’ ‘That is the man we deported to the UK in 2010 after discovering he is among Islamic radicals who were recruited to train as Al Shabaab in Somalia three years ago.’ Kenyan government spokesman Muthui Kariuki said: ‘We handed him to British security agents in Kenya and he seems to have found his way to London and mutated to Michael Adebolajo. The Kenyan government cannot be held responsible for what happened to him after we handed him to British authorities.’ After their arrest, Adebolajo, the five others, the guest house owners and the worker, were taken to Mombasa and spent several days in prison before appearing before a magistrate. Kenyan detectives suspected Adebolajo may have been a ringleader because he was most vocal in court and appeared to know how to ‘play the system’. In court, he claimed: ‘We are being tortured by police and we haven’t eaten for two days now. We have been denied the right to talk to our family members and lawyer. We are being treated as criminals and we are innocent.’ The court instructed police to build a case within three days, but after the British embassy's assurance of Adebolajo's clean record, he was deported. Another Kenyan source accused the British of failing to help them build a case against Adebolajo, stating: ‘It was a major anti-terror investigation and we were given three days by the courts to build up a case.’ The Foreign Office confirmed Adebolajo had been arrested in 2010 and that it provided consular assistance ‘as normal’ in the circumstances. A Foreign Office statement read: ‘We can confirm a British national was arrested in Kenya in 2010. The Foreign and Commonwealth Office provided consular assistance as normal for British nationals.’

It is believed that the Kenyan cleric Sheikh Aboud Rogo – who was killed by gunmen in Mombasa the previous year – had helped to fund the men. article_content: An extraordinary 'bayonet hat,' designed to allow British soldiers in World War I to attack with their heads, has surfaced nearly a century after being rejected. This rare prototype, featuring a sharp six-inch blade fixed to the top, was deemed too dangerous by the War Office. The hat is now expected to fetch over £3,000 at auction. The 'bayonet hat' was conceived by British solicitor Philip Baker, who aimed to enable soldiers to stab enemies by ramming them head-first or using the hat as a conventional knife. Baker patented the invention in 1916 and presented a prototype and drawings to the War Office. The design included a scabbard to cover the blade and a locking mechanism for use in trenches. In close combat, soldiers could flick the knife upwards and use it alongside their rifle and bayonet. The plan was to modify both army caps and steel helmets, with the latter serving as a shield and the dagger as a handle. However, the War Office rejected the bayonet cap due to safety concerns. The hat was one of many unusual weapon inventions created during World War I to give British soldiers an advantage. The prototype, complete with the fixed knife, is being auctioned on June 25, accompanied by the original patent document and drawings. Matthew Tredwin of C&T Auctioneers described it as a 'barbaric weapon' and noted the rarity of such unproduced items. The hat was previously held by the Wilson Military Headgear History Research Centre in the US, founded by the late Robert Wilson. Terry Charman of the Imperial War Museum characterized it as one of the 'weird and wonderful' inventions of the era, designed to aid British soldiers in hand-to-hand combat. The article also provides brief information about other WWI inventions: Tanks: The British Mark I tank, designed in 1915, first saw combat at the Somme in September 1916. Flamethrowers: First used by German troops in February 1915, flamethrowers project streams of fire and were used in fortifications. Aircraft Carriers: The HMS Furious, originally a battle cruiser, began its conversion into the first aircraft carrier during World War I. Air Traffic Control: Developed during the war, with the first two-way radio in planes and the first air traffic control at Croydon Airport in 1921.

article_content: In Moscow, Russia, the iconic St. Basil's Cathedral, famous for its vibrant, onion-shaped domes, has been recreated as an edible masterpiece. Troman Felizmenio, a talented pastry chef, has crafted a gingerbread version of the landmark specifically for the festive holiday period. Felizmenio is employed at the Ritz Carlton, which is situated close to both the Kremlin and Red Square. According to the hotel, the construction of this sweet cathedral, which stands at an impressive 2 meters (6.5 feet) high, commenced in early September and spanned almost three months. Felizmenio dedicated two to three hours daily to assembling the elaborate structure. The chef emphasized in a press release the critical importance of maintaining accurate proportions when constructing gingerbread structures of this magnitude. Without precise proportions, the entire edifice risks collapse, a fate that even the binding power of melted sugar cannot avert. This gingerbread rendition of St. Basil's Cathedral is prominently displayed in the hotel lobby. Felizmenio’s confectionery creation replicates the precise dimensions and external features of the original 16th-century cathedral. It boasts a central tower and eight surrounding towers, each topped with an onion dome and lavishly adorned with royal icing. History tells us that Ivan the Terrible, the Tsar of Muscovy, commissioned the building of St. Basil's Cathedral to commemorate his military triumph over Kazan in 1552. Kazan, located east of Moscow, was then a stronghold of the Tatars, a Turkic ethnic group. Each dome shelters a chapel, which symbolizes a specific assault made by Ivan during the siege of Kazan. In the 1580s, a ninth tower was erected to house the tomb of St. Basil the Blessed. Felizmenio and his team are producing a limited quantity of smaller, commercially available versions of the gingerbread cathedral, priced from 50,000 rubles (approximately $1,600). CNN's Max Tkachenko and Deb Krajnak contributed to this news report.

article_content: A video appearing to show a young woman throwing live puppies into a river has sparked widespread outrage online. This incident has prompted an animal rights group to offer a reward for information leading to the arrest of those responsible. People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals (PETA) is offering a reward for information that leads to the capture and arrest of the individuals behind what they describe as a 'heinous act' of cruelty. 'Animal abusers are cowards,' stated PETA Manager Martin Mersereau in a news release announcing the $2,000 reward. 'They often take out their issues on the most defenseless beings,' he added. The video depicts a girl in a red hooded sweatshirt throwing at least six puppies into a fast-moving river. She seems to be speaking Croatian while repeatedly taking live puppies from a bucket and throwing them into the water. The fate of the puppies remains unclear. CNN has not been able to independently verify the authenticity of the video. The video was initially posted on YouTube but was quickly removed. However, it is still widely available online and has become viral, with sites like LiveLeak.com reporting over 1.3 million views of the footage. Web users have organized on sites such as 4chan.org to help identify the woman and the man who filmed the incident. PETA suggests that clues in the video and the original post indicate it may have been filmed near the Vrbas River in Bosnia-Herzegovina. A Facebook page created to help track down the individuals involved has gained over 7,000 followers since the video was posted on Monday. Users of the 4chan.org site recently gained attention for identifying the person behind a similar incident involving a British woman who was filmed throwing a cat into a trash can last week.

article_content: A robber has been jailed after a series of street robberies targeting women for their gold necklaces. Ralf Dautzenberg, 22, was captured on CCTV grabbing a woman from behind and stealing her necklace in Hayes, west London. This attack was part of a six-month crime spree where he stole approximately £20,000 worth of jewellery. Dautzenberg pleaded guilty to 11 counts of robbery and one count of theft at Isleworth Crown Court and was sentenced to six years in prison. Detectives reported that Dautzenberg would approach his victims from behind, often using violence, to steal gold necklaces. One victim shared her ongoing fear and trauma resulting from the incident. Police investigations revealed that Dautzenberg used public transportation to identify and follow potential victims. Detective Chief Inspector Richard Turner commended the investigation team's work. The police emphasized their commitment to combating Asian gold theft and supporting victims of violence.

article_content: Rumors suggest Samsung is developing a smartwatch that functions independently of a phone. Patent images indicate it may even forgo a touchscreen. The Korean firm's patent application details a standalone smartwatch controlled via gestures, detected by embedded sensors. These sensors would recognize movements such as flicks and waves. The application mentions a depth sensor combined with a camera that could identify what the user is pointing at. Patent images illustrate a potential Samsung smartwatch incorporating sensors to detect hand movements. Samsung may be entering the virtual reality market with a headset reportedly in development. Prototypes have been allegedly sent to developers for testing, with a possible launch later this year. Sources claim the headsets will feature OLED screens and connect to future Galaxy devices. Reports suggest the headset will operate on Android, not Tizen, Samsung's smartwatch OS. Orientation sensors could unlock the device or launch apps with a wrist flick. Ambient sounds picked up by the microphone could contextualize gestures; for example, at a concert, a camera gesture could switch to video mode. The patent states a depth sensor with a camera can enhance environment detection and identify the object a user interacts with. Sensors might include inertial or orientation sensors like accelerometers, gyroscopes, magnetometers, GPS chips, or compasses. Earlier patent filings this week described a Samsung smartwatch needing no phone to operate. Samsung has four smartwatches, including the Android-powered Galaxy Gear and the Tizen-powered Gear 2. The new smartwatch's OS is currently unknown. Sensors can activate the device, detect gestures, or interact with content on the device's screen. Microphones can detect speech or ambient sounds to understand the device's context. Existing products like the Galaxy S5 already have gesture controls and sensors. The upcoming smartwatch could enhance these. The patent indicates sensors will activate the device, detect gestures, and interact with content. Samsung plans to unveil the smartwatch soon to capture more of the wearable technology market. According to sources, the smartwatch will take photos, send emails, monitor heart rate, and use GPS tracking. The name, cost, and call functionality remain undisclosed. The patent suggests a round face, similar to the Moto 360.

article_content: After acknowledging her past as 'the most humiliated woman in the world,' Monica Lewinsky is stepping back into the public eye, mingling with celebrities and royalty. However, her recent appearance at London's Mayfair hotspot, Little House, might be ill-timed, as MailOnline reports Hillary Clinton is arriving in the city. Clinton, a potential presidential candidate and one-time figure connected to Lewinsky, is traveling to London to promote her latest book, 'Hard Choices.' Lewinsky has decided to no longer remain hidden, declaring, 'It's time to burn the beret and bury the blue dress,' signaling a desire to move forward. Clinton is engaging fully with the media during her visit, including an appearance on Jeremy Vine's BBC Radio 2 lunchtime show and an interview on Radio 4's Woman's Hour. Prior to her UK departure, Clinton shared a photo on Twitter of herself signing copies of 'Hard Choices' at Hudson News in New York's JFK airport. Meanwhile, Lewinsky, now 40, was spotted looking stylish at Soho House, a members-only club in London. This suggests she was invited by a prominent member. After a decade of self-imposed exile, Lewinsky aims to redefine her narrative beyond the affair with President Bill Clinton. She recently attended the Masterpiece Marie Curie party, engaging with figures like Princess Beatrice, Clive Owen, and Yasmin Le Bon, supporting the Marie Curie Cancer Care charity. In a recent Vanity Fair article, Lewinsky broke her silence, stating her deep regret for the affair and her determination to move on. Lewinsky also discusses being 'the most humiliated woman in the world' in a new National Geographic documentary, 'The 90s: The Last Great Decade?', set to air soon. The timing of Lewinsky's return coincides with the release of Clinton's memoir, fueling speculation about a potential 2016 presidential run. Lewinsky says she is no longer willing to put her life on hold. Clinton claims she has 'moved on' from the scandal and encourages others to do the same. She also acknowledged reading Lewinsky's Vanity Fair essay. However, Republicans have indicated that the scandal remains relevant in the context of political discourse. Lewinsky hopes to leverage her experiences to assist others facing public humiliation, inspired by the tragedy of Tyler Clementi. She aims to advocate for victims of online harassment and speak publicly on the issue.

article_content: Feeling overwhelmed by work and unable to find time for a few days off, with your work-life balance suffering? If you're an American worker, this may be the case. A recent study revealed that U.S. workers forfeited $52.4 billion in time-off benefits in 2013 and took less vacation time than in the past four decades. American workers forwent a total of 169 million days of paid time off, effectively 'providing free labor for their employers at an average of $504 per employee,' according to the study. The study, titled 'All Work and No Pay: The Impact of Forfeited Time Off,' was conducted by Oxford Economics for the U.S. Travel Association's Travel Effect Initiative, examining the impact of forgone vacation time. 'Americans are work martyrs,' the U.S. Travel Association states. 'Tied to the office, they leave more paid time off unused each year, forfeiting their earned benefits and essentially working for free.' The study indicated that in 2013, U.S. employees took an average of 16 vacation days, compared to 20.3 days in 2000. The travel association suggests that 'returning to pre-2000 vacation patterns would have a massive economic potential: annual vacation days taken by U.S. employees would increase by 27% (or 768 million days), delivering a $284 billion impact across the U.S. economy.' The association is a national nonprofit organization based in Washington, D.C., representing all components of the travel industry. Does this resonate with you? Productivity and stress management coach Joe Robinson identifies several factors driving this issue. 'Workers are afraid to take vacations in the layoff era,' Robinson explained. 'It could portray them as less committed than their coworkers. This is known as defensive overworking; they work long hours and skip vacations to protect themselves from cutbacks.' According to Roger Dow, president and CEO of the U.S. Travel Association, 28% of surveyed workers admitted to declining earned days off to demonstrate job dedication. Dow explained, 'They don't want to be seen as slackers and want to be perceived as highly dedicated.' However, this is often counterproductive. People who take more time off tend to receive more raises and promotions. Robinson concurred, 'It's futile. Those who don't take vacations are just as likely to be laid off.' Workforce reductions and 'device addiction' are other contributing factors. 'Lean staffing, where individuals handle the responsibilities of multiple roles, makes it difficult to disconnect,' Robinson noted. 'Employees are not taking vacations because of excessive workloads.' Dow noted that 'approximately 40% of surveyed workers fear the amount of accumulated work awaiting them upon their return from vacation. The prospect of a work pileup is daunting.' Robinson added, 'Another significant reason people don't take time off is their immersion in busyness and device addiction. Many individuals equate their worth with their productivity, leading to guilt when they step away.' Can this trend be reversed? Some studies suggest that reduced vacation time can lead to decreased productivity. Researcher Mark Rosekind of Alertness Solutions discovered that the respite effect of a vacation could boost performance by 80%. Reaction times among returning vacationers improved by 40% in his study. Dow mentioned that certain U.S. companies, particularly on the West Coast, are starting to revise their vacation policies. 'Several companies, including Expedia and Netflix, are experimenting with unlimited vacation policies,' Dow stated. 'They've simply said, discuss your time off needs with your manager and take the necessary time.' Additionally, companies with 'use it or lose it' policies, which prevent the rollover of annual vacation time, observe higher rates of employees utilizing their earned leave. Dow also mentioned that some companies, including the U.S. Travel Association, are now offering bonuses to employees who use their full allotment of paid leave. These companies may be convinced by the growing research supporting the long-term benefits of time away from work. Robinson, author of 'Work to Live' and 'Don't Miss Your Life,' also penned an Entrepreneur magazine article titled 'The Secret to Increased Productivity: Taking Time Off,' where he argues that 'working without breaks is detrimental to business, health, and the life you're working towards.' Have you forfeited earned time off? Are you satisfied with your time away from work? Share your experiences in the comments.

article_content: In 1968, at just 21, Henning Frunder sought to escape Eastern Germany. A planned sea journey with other students, facilitated by Polish fishermen aiming for West Germany's northern border, never materialized. His letters requesting funds for the escape, sent to Western friends, were intercepted by the Stasi, East Germany's secret police. Consequently, Frunder and his companions faced arrest, trial, and imprisonment for attempting to illegally leave the country. Frunder spent several months incarcerated by the Stasi before being deported to West Germany in 1970. At the time, the identity of the informant remained unknown. 'We lacked conspiratorial training and perhaps placed too much trust in others,' he reflected. It was clear to Frunder that the betrayal originated from someone they considered a friend. For over four decades, the Stasi conducted extensive surveillance on East German citizens, frequently employing 'informal employees' – secret informants – to monitor colleagues, friends, and even family. As the Berlin Wall fell in November 1989, Stasi operatives received orders to destroy evidence, including informant names, records of Western dealings, trial protocols, and recordings. This information was never intended for public view. However, activists intervened, occupying the Stasi headquarters in January 1990 and halting the destruction. Over 45 million pages of Stasi files, many torn by hand or shredded, were recovered. More than 15,000 bags containing over 600 million paper fragments were salvaged. In 1992, following German reunification, the Agency for the Federal Commission for the Stasi Records (BStU) was established to address this immense historical puzzle. Roland Jahn, a former Stasi prisoner himself, heads the Stasi Records Agency. He underscores the agency's vital role in grappling with the past. 'Access to these files is incredibly important for those affected, as it restores a stolen part of their lives,' Jahn emphasizes. He notes the agency's unique function in providing access to secret police files, setting an international example. To date, 1.5 million pieces have been reassembled, largely by hand. Currently, a small team is dedicated to manually reconstructing the files. Considering the remaining 600 million pieces, continuing manually seems nearly impossible. 'Developing systems to accelerate this process is crucial,' Jahn asserts. A computer system introduced in 2007 has aided in reconstructing four bags thus far. Addressing the remaining 15,000 bags requires 'better scanning technology,' according to Jahn. Decades after his betrayal, Henning Frunder believed he had moved on and dismissed the possibility of identifying his denouncer. 'I stopped wondering and thought it would not change much,' he recalls. In 1994, he received initial clues about the potential betrayer, but it wasn't until 2011, more than five decades later, that the Stasi Records Agency contacted him. 'They found a bag with my name from among 15,000,' he recounts. The file belonged to Aleksander Radler, a Stasi informant nicknamed 'Thomas,' who was a member of Frunder's student group and had spied for over 25 years. 'Learning that Radler was living in Sweden as a priest, preaching, sparked my outrage,' Frunder says. However, Frunder never reached out to Radler. 'He never expressed remorse; had he done so, a conversation might have been interesting.' Despite the resurfacing of painful memories, Frunder believes reconstructing the Stasi files is beneficial for society. 'Reflecting on my own story, I managed because I was young and hadn't accumulated much to lose. But others suffered more, and many have significant gaps in their experiences that reconstructing Stasi files could help fill,' he adds. Stasi Records Agency Commissioner Roland Jahn views confronting the past as essential for the future. 'Choosing to live with a lie harms our democracy. Therefore, uncovering the truth is vital, even if it's painful,' he states. Today, individuals can request access to their Stasi files online or in person. Over the past two decades, more than three million file requests have been submitted, with over 30,000 in 2014 alone. Jahn cannot predict when the remaining 600 million pieces of Stasi files will be reassembled. It depends on funding, public and political interest, and technological advancements. Nevertheless, Jahn expresses pride in the accomplishments of the past 25 years. 'Germany has demonstrated how to consistently confront and address its past, setting an important international example.'

article_content: An Indiana woman who rescued a baby squirrel after its nest was accidentally chainsawed is being asked to give him up. Sara Householder has cared for Rocky the squirrel since March, after a tree surgeon sawed through his nest, killing his mother. Having fed him formula from a syringe since he was a few days old, Householder may have to hand Rocky over to authorities because she lacks the required license. Inspectors visited the house and reported the squirrel is healthy. The issue came to light when Householder attempted to obtain a license after acquiring the animal. The Department of Natural Resources says she violated regulations and must hand Rocky over to a licensed animal rehabilitator by next week. Householder tearfully told WANE TV, 'I raised him from an infant. I fed him through a syringe every two hours. I will do whatever it takes to keep my baby.' The incident occurred while Householder's mother-in-law was having trees removed. Householder initially took in the squirrel out of compassion. The squirrel is kept in a cage in Householder's Fort Wayne, Indiana, home. Rocky's favorite snack is Reese's Pieces, which Householder feeds him. She said, 'I couldn't leave him to die; he was only a few days old. I wasn't going to leave him in the freezing cold in March.' She grew attached to Rocky, bought him a cage, and feeds him Reese's Pieces. He is now part of the family and gets along with other pets. An Animal Care and Control officer inspected Rocky and found him to be fine. Phil Bloom, a spokesman for the Department of Natural Resources, said, 'If someone feels the need to save an animal, the proper procedure is to turn it over to a licensed wild animal rehabilitator within 24 hours.' Rocky is allowed to roam the living room and interacts well with the family's other animals. Householder says she will do 'whatever it takes to get my baby back.'

article_content: The head of the Papua New Guinea military has been freed from detention by rebel soldiers, the Australian government said Thursday, after an attempted mutiny appeared to unravel. Yaura Sasa, the rebel commander, had earlier claimed that he had seized control of the Papua New Guinea Defence Force, confining its leader, Brig. Gen. Francis Agwi, and another senior officer, to their residences. The Australian government -- which has a significant presence in Papua New Guinea, a country it previously administered -- said that Agwi had subsequently been released. The Australian Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade said in a statement that it was important that 'order be fully restored' within the Papua New Guinea armed forces. The unrest in the military stemmed from controversy in Papua New Guinea over the legitimate prime minister. Sasa claimed he had taken control of the defence force in order 'to restore integrity and respect for the constitution and judiciary'. He called for the immediate implementation of 'the supreme court decision relating to Sir Michael Somare's position as prime minister of Papua New Guinea'. Somare has been a key figure in Papua New Guinea's political landscape for four decades, having helped lead the country to independence in the 1970s. After intermittently holding office, he was elected prime minister in 2007. He lost his position last year while recovering from heart surgery in Singapore. He now disputes the legitimacy of the current prime minister, Peter O'Neill. In a news briefing, O'Neill described the events at the military barracks as 'completely unnecessary'. He blamed Somare for the disturbances. 'We condemn the actions of particularly the Somare faction of our Parliament for creating an environment where instability is being fostered within the country and the disciplined forces,' he said. The Australian government said O'Neill had told Ian Kemish, the Australian high commissioner in Port Moresby, that the authorities 'were taking steps to manage the situation' in the military barracks. CNN's Jethro Mullen contributed to this report.

article_content: Researchers have uncovered details about how different types of dinosaurs shared food resources, allowing them to live together in tough prehistoric environments. The study focused on large, long-necked, plant-eating dinosaurs called sauropods, like Diplodocus, which dominated the land between 210 million and 65 million years ago and needed massive amounts of food. These sauropods were the biggest land animals ever, with some weighing as much as 80 tonnes. Scientists analysed dinosaur skulls to figure out how these massive creatures divided up their food, helping them to co-exist in challenging prehistoric ecosystems. A completed skull model of Camarasaurus, a sauropod from Late Jurassic North America, is shown. Researchers from the University of Bristol and the Natural History Museum in London suggest that different sauropod species could live in the same areas because they ate different things. The Late Jurassic Morrison Formation, a distinctive sequence of sedimentary rock in the western United States, contained more than 10 species of sauropods. In contrast, modern African ecosystems, which are highly diverse, only support one gigantic species: the elephant. Experts examined digital models of the skulls, jaws, and neck muscles of two sauropods, Camarasaurus and Diplodocus, to see how they ate. The skull model is shown from various angles. Researchers used these models to determine the size and structure of the dinosaurs' teeth. The University of Bristol and the Natural History Museum in London studied sauropod skulls found in the Morrison Formation, which extends throughout the Western United States. The skulls of Camarasaurus (left) and Diplodocus (right) were digitally reconstructed to study their feeding methods. The top skulls show a reconstructed jaw. The bottom image uses colour to show areas of higher stress when biting. David Button, a PhD student at Bristol's School of Earth Sciences, explained that while neither dinosaur could chew, their skulls were effective at cropping plants. Camarasaurus had a strong skull and bite, which allowed it to eat tough leaves and branches. Diplodocus, on the other hand, had a weaker bite and a more delicate skull, limiting it to softer foods like ferns. A primitive meat-eating dinosaur from about 200 million years ago was discovered in South America. This new species, named Tachiraptor admirabilis, was about the size of a lion and found in the Venezuelan Andes. It was an ancestor of well-known dinosaurs like Tyrannosaurus Rex, Velociraptor, and Spinosaurus. Over 6ft (1.8 metres) long, it is one of the few dinosaurs ever recovered from northern South America and the first carnivorous member of the group discovered in Venezuela. At that time, all the Earth’s land was connected in one supercontinent called Pangaea, surrounded by a huge ocean. Pangaea was just starting to break apart into the continents we know today. Tachiraptor was around at the beginning of the period known geologically as the Jurassic, and helps explain the spread of carnivorous dinosaurs following the Triassic mass extinction shortly before. Half the world’s animals were mysteriously wiped out by either climate change, volcanic eruptions or an asteroid impact. Tachiraptor's fossilised shinbone and hipbone were found together, and analysis showed it was a different species from others. The study published in the journal Royal Society Open Science said. Diplodocus could have also used its strong neck muscles to pull plants apart. This indicates differences in diet between the two dinosaurs, which would have allowed them to co-exist. The researchers also used biomechanical measurements from other sauropod species to calculate the difference in movement in their skulls and jaws. They found that other Morrison Formation sauropods were also highly varied in feeding adaptations, which suggests they had different diets. Large, long-necked, plant-eating dinosaurs, such as Diplodocus, dominated the land between 210 million and 65 million years ago and would have needed huge amounts of food. Professor Emily Rayfield of the University of Bristol explained that in modern animal communities, differences in diet allow similar species to live together by reducing competition for food. This is termed dietary niche partitioning. Although dietary niche partitioning has been suspected between Morrison Formation sauropods based on their structural features and patterns of tooth-wear, this is the first study to provide strong, numerical, biomechanical evidence for its presence in this fossil community. Professor Paul Barrett of the Natural History Museum added that this study provides insight not only into the ecology of dinosaurs but more generally into the mechanisms supporting species-richness in other animal communities, both from the fossil record and in the present day. The research, funded by the Natural Environment Research Council, was published in the journal Proceedings of the Royal Society B.

article_content: Topshop is challenging a court decision that prevents them from selling a T-shirt featuring Rihanna's image. The clothing retailer has filed an appeal after a previous ruling prohibited the sale of the shirt, triggered by concerns that customers might mistakenly believe Rihanna had given her approval. The legal dispute arose when a High Court judge sided with Rihanna, suggesting that fans could be misled into thinking she endorsed Topshop's 'tank' top. Consequently, the shirt was ordered to be removed from stores. Topshop, owned by Sir Philip Green's Arcadia Group, is now seeking a review by appeal judges at the Royal Courts of Justice in London, arguing that the initial legal interpretation regarding celebrity merchandising was flawed. During the original case, Rihanna's legal team pointed out that the T-shirt image came from an unauthorized photograph taken in 2011 while she was filming a music video in Northern Ireland. The judge agreed that Topshop's sale of the shirt without Rihanna's consent constituted 'passing off,' an act of misrepresentation. Topshop's legal representative, Geoffrey Hobbs QC, presented a collection of the contested T-shirts to the appeal judges, emphasizing that the case involved a common practice of using star images for merchandising, similar to those of Elvis Presley, Jimi Hendrix, and Prince. Hobbs claimed that Rihanna was attempting to use 'passing off' law to monopolize the marketing of her own identity. Rihanna has endorsement deals with companies like River Island, a competitor of Topshop. Topshop argues that the public doesn't automatically assume that clothing images are always authorized by the celebrities they feature. Legal expert Mike Gardner from Wedlake Bell LLP noted that in the UK, celebrities lack a general legal right to control their image. However, marketing a product in a way that incorrectly implies endorsement can be considered illegal 'passing off.' Gardner suggested that if Topshop loses the appeal, other retailers might be wary of selling similar items, potentially leading celebrities to more aggressively protect their image rights. Conversely, a Topshop victory could force celebrities to rethink their branding strategies in countries with limited image rights. The appeal case is ongoing, and comments are currently disabled on the article.

article_content: Kim Yuna, a prominent South Korean star, secured her nation's first figure skating gold medal at the Vancouver Winter Olympics in 2010. Affectionately known as 'Queen Yuna' by her devoted fans, the 20-year-old is far from the aloof persona her nickname might imply. She headlines sold-out ice dancing performances and endorses numerous products, capitalizing on her wholesome public image. Kim Yuna also hosts the TV program 'Kiss and Cry,' a South Korean adaptation of 'Dancing with the Stars' on ice, which she hopes will promote the sport in South Korea. 'It brings me great joy to see the participants enjoying themselves,' she stated. 'Even though some occasionally get injured, they enjoy it immensely, and I hope the show inspires viewers to try it themselves.' Recognized by TIME magazine as one of the 100 most influential people of 2010, Kim Yuna began training as an ice skater at age 5. At 16, she relocated to Toronto to pursue her Olympic aspirations. Her dedication culminated in a gold medal at the Vancouver Olympics, where she achieved a record-breaking score of 228.56 points in women's figure skating. This was the highest score recorded since the International Skating Union (ISU) judging system was implemented. She surpassed her own world record and outscored her closest competitor, Mao Asada of Japan, by a significant 23.06 points. Having now won every 'grand slam' title in figure skating, including the World Grand Prix Final, Four Continents Championships, and World Championships, Kim Yuna is among the world's highest-paid athletes, according to Forbes magazine. In addition to her competitive skating career, she serves as an ambassador for South Korea's bid to host the 2018 Winter Olympics in Pyeongchang. This role makes her even more anxious than competing at the Olympics. 'I felt like my heart would burst during the presentation in Lausanne, Switzerland. The nervousness was unparalleled compared to my performances,' she explained. 'Previously, I only focused on my own endeavors. However, this represents the aspirations of many Koreans, and the thought of bearing the nation's expectations, even alongside others, caused me great worry and unease.' CNN interviewed Kim Yuna at the Blush bar located within the Grand InterContinental Seoul Parnas.

article_content: By Emily Allen Last updated at 12:38 PM on 29th February 2012 The number of British women dying from breast cancer has fallen by more than 10 percent in five years. The death rate from the disease is now on par with or lower than France and Germany, according to Italian and Swiss researchers. Ten years ago, the UK's death rate from the disease was higher than France, Germany, Italy, Poland, and Spain. Scientists say the death rate has fallen fastest among those under 50, claiming better treatment and not screening appears to be the reason. However, although British women with breast cancer now have a better chance of beating the disease, the country still lags behind the European average. Scientists say the death rate has fallen fastest among those under 50, claiming better treatment and not screening appears to be the reason for the decline. They said deaths will continue falling this year to 15.95 per 100,000 women compared to 18.39 per 100,000 women in 2007. This represents a drop of approximately 13 percent over five years. UK: -10.64% SPAIN: -9.21% FRANCE: -8.89% ITALY: -7.71% GERMANY: -7.15% POLAND: -2.48% EU OVERALL: -8.44% However, the UK is still shy of the European average of 14.9 deaths per 100,000 women. Spain tops the league, with fewer than 12 deaths per 100,000 people predicted. The findings were published in the journal Annals of Oncology after researchers studied cancer rates in 27 member states of the EU using World Health Organisation (WHO) data. Spain tops the league, with fewer than 12 deaths per 100,000 people predicted to die of breast cancer. Dr Rachel Greig, of the charity Breakthrough Breast Cancer, said that it was 'reassuring' to see that the number of deaths from the disease could fall at a time when the number of women contracting the disease is increasing. She said 12,000 women a year were still dying of the disease in Britain. Professor Carlo La Vecchia, one of the study leaders from the University of Milan, told the Daily Telegraph that the figures show 'important advancements in treatment and management are playing a major role in the decline in death rates'. A Department of Health spokesman said more than £750 million was being invested to help diagnose cancer earlier and provide people with access to the latest treatments in order to save 5,000 more lives a year by 2015.

article_content: The parents of a 17-year-old football player have filed a $3 million lawsuit against a school, alleging that a teacher performed a sex act on the student after a pep rally. Symone Greene, 22, was arrested last week on charges related to having sex with the student on her first day teaching at Options Public Charter School in Washington, D.C. The parents claim that the school and the private company that hired Greene failed to adequately ensure she would not prey on vulnerable students under her care, according to WRC-TV reports. Greene is also named in the lawsuit. Symone Greene, 22, is accused of performing a sex act on a 17-year-old student in her classroom on her first day of school. Greene is charged with first-degree sexual abuse of a minor because she held a position of authority as the student's teacher. Authorities state that the teen, a football player, recorded Greene performing a sex act on him after a high school pep rally. The parents assert that their son has a learning disability and that Greene took advantage of him on October 17, when she allegedly engaged in sexual relations with him in an empty classroom following the pep rally. The lawsuit claims that Greene initiated the flirting that preceded the alleged sexual encounter and that another teacher witnessed the flirting but did not intervene. The teen told police that he had 'flirted' with the teacher earlier on October 17 and sent her a text message inquiring if she was 'kinky.' According to Governor Jackson, the lawyer representing the boy's family, these details are inconsequential. He told WRC, 'Even if that young man entered the classroom wearing only boxers and behaved even more provocatively than alleged, the teacher had a duty to intervene, report the behavior to the appropriate authorities, and uphold the standards expected of teachers in our society.' The alleged sex act occurred at the end of the school's pep rally, purportedly in Greene's classroom, where the student recorded the act without her knowledge, according to the warrant. Greene allegedly sent the teen a text message over the weekend, asking him to keep the incident secret because 'it is not right for a student and teacher to have a relationship.' The student recorded the sexual encounter without Greene's knowledge, and he then shared the video with his football teammates and other friends. Symone Greene, 22, was working at Options Public Charter School in Northeast D.C. when she first met the victim, according to court documents. She also allegedly sent a clothed picture of herself to the student, WUSA reports. According to a statement from Shannon Hodge, the school's executive director, 'When school administrators learned of the incident Monday morning, we immediately contacted the Child and Family Services Agency, the Metropolitan Police Department, and the parent of the student.' Hodge stated that Greene was contracted through a Delaware-based company and had not previously worked at the school. Greene was arrested and charged this week, according to the documents.

article_content: The daily walk to school can be challenging for many children. However, consider the plight of these young pupils and their parents as they navigate their way to classes. At the newly-opened £4 million Chaddesley Corbett primary school in Worcestershire, students must wade through mud because a pedestrian footpath was not constructed. Parents, comparing the situation to the aftermath of a rainy festival, have expressed their anger regarding the absence of a suitable access route to the school. The primary school opened only recently, and following heavy rainfall, the path to the school has become churned up, leaving children dirty before they even arrive and making it difficult for parents with strollers to reach the school. Three-year-old Isabelle Foreman looks at her muddy shoes as her mother, Kate, walks her along the path. Mother-of-two Kate Foreman, 31, with Isabelle, 3, and Poppy, 11 weeks, makes her way along the muddy path leading to the brand new Chaddesley Corbett Endowed Primary School, which opened this week. Despite the £4 million investment in the school, parents have criticized the lack of pedestrian access for students and their families. Kate Foreman, 31, stated that taking her three-year-old daughter Isabelle to school for her first day was a nightmare. She commented: 'It's a mud bath, like the end of a music festival. People without cars who have to walk to school won't be able to get there. You need wellies and waterproofs, it's that bad. You have no chance if you have a stroller; the wheels would get stuck.' She added: 'It's a complete oversight. They spent all that money on the school but didn't consider how people would get there.' Kate Foreman says that she and her daughter Isabelle will need to wear wellies and waterproofs to get to school. The new school features larger classrooms, a hall, forest school areas, and dedicated facilities for food technology, music, and science. The school is the result of a merger between two existing schools: Chaddesley Corbett Endowed First School and the nearby Stone First School. Plans for the school were criticized when approved last year by the local highways authority and local ramblers, who argued that excessive car parking would encourage car dependence for students getting to school. Councillor Stephen Clee stated that Worcestershire County Council is seeking a short-term solution to the issue. He said: 'We fully appreciate the concerns of parents about the current condition of the path leading to the school. I have been working with officers in our countryside service, the parish council, and the landowner to provide a short-term improvement to the path that will help parents and children get to and from the new school safely.' Worcestershire County Council described pedestrian access to the school as a ‘rural footpath.’ Chaddesley Corbett is an 'Aided School,' meaning it is owned by Trustees rather than the county council. The Trustees acquired the land for the new school, and subsequently, the local authority supported the trustees through their planning application and provided funding for the construction. The council noted that a condition of the planning permission submitted by the Trustees of the school to Wyre Forest District Council was to provide improvements to the footpath accessing the rear of the school, and this work should have been completed by the applicant. Worcestershire County Council reported that a landowner, believed to be a garden nursery adjacent to the site, has pledged to carry out improvements to the path. The path, running alongside neighboring nurseries, is the only pedestrian access to the new school site. The construction of Chaddesley Corbett Primary School cost £4 million and involved the merger of two smaller local schools.
